title: From Maryam to Al-Furqan
intro: 34 days through surahs 19 to 25, from Maryam to Al-Furqan, one verse at a time.

posts.caption: This plan walks through surahs 19 to 25, starting with Maryam, a Meccan surah of 98 verses named after Mary, the mother of the Prophet Isa (Jesus). It is the only surah named after a woman, and she is the only woman named in the Quran. It opens with the aged Prophet Zakariyya (Zechariah) praying quietly for a child.

Maryam (Mary), alone and in the pains of childbirth, rests against the trunk of a palm tree. A voice comforts her and points her to a stream and to ripe dates. Classical commentators differ on whose voice it was: the angel Jibril (Gabriel), or the newborn Prophet Isa (Jesus) himself.

When her people accuse Maryam (Mary), she points to her baby, and the Prophet Isa (Jesus) speaks from the cradle. He calls himself a servant of Allah and a prophet, and ends with these words. Earlier in the surah, almost the same words of peace are spoken of the Prophet Yahya (John the Baptist).

The Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) has gently urged his father to leave idol worship, and his father threatens to stone him and sends him away. Ibrahim answers with peace and a promise to pray for him. Four times in this passage he addresses him as ya abati, a tender way of saying "O my father".

"Love" here translates the Arabic wudd, a warm and lasting affection, from the same root as al-Wadud, "the Loving", one of the names of Allah. Classical commentators such as Ibn Kathir explain it as love that Allah places for the righteous in the hearts of others.

posts.display: We have not revealed unto thee (Muhammad) this Qur'an that thou shouldst be distressed, But as a reminder unto him who feareth.
posts.caption: Ta-Ha, a Meccan surah of 135 verses, is named after the two Arabic letters that open it. Some commentators read them as a name of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and Taha is a common given name among Muslims. These first lines reassure him that the Quran was not sent to bring him distress.

The Prophet Musa (Moses), travelling with his family, sees a fire in the distance and goes to it hoping for a burning brand or someone to show the way. There he is called by name. Tuwa is the sacred valley, and commentators explain removing the shoes as a sign of humility and reverence.

The Prophet Musa (Moses) has just been told to go to Pharaoh, and he answers with this prayer for courage and clear speech. Many Muslims recite it before an exam, a talk or a difficult conversation. "Relieve my mind" renders the Arabic ishrah li sadri, literally "expand my chest".

Allah sends the Prophets Musa (Moses) and Harun (Aaron) to Pharaoh, a ruler the Quran describes as a tyrant, and tells them to speak to him gently. Commentators often cite it as a model for speaking with kindness, even to someone deep in wrongdoing. "Peradventure" means "perhaps".

Pharaoh demands to know who this Lord of theirs is, and the Prophet Musa (Moses) answers in a single line: the One who gave every created thing its form and nature, then guided it on its way. It is one of the Quran's most compact descriptions of creation and guidance.

The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is told not to hurry to repeat the Quran before each revelation is complete. Then comes a short prayer, rabbi zidni ilma, "My Lord, increase me in knowledge", one of the best-loved prayers among Muslims and a favourite of students. "Ere" means "before".

Al-Anbiya, "The Prophets", is a Meccan surah of 112 verses that recalls a long line of prophets, among them Musa (Moses), Ibrahim (Abraham) and Yunus (Jonah). This verse is a plain reminder that every life ends, and that both hardship and ease are a test. The same phrase about tasting death appears in two other surahs.

posts.display: We said: O fire, be coolness and peace for Abraham.
posts.caption: The young Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) has broken his people's idols, and they throw him into a fire. Allah commands the fire itself to be cool and safe for him. Some classical commentators note that "and peace" was added so that the fire would not become harmfully cold either.

The Prophet Ayyub (Job) is remembered in Islam as a model of sabr, patient endurance, through long illness and loss. His prayer is famously gentle: he does not complain or demand, he simply names his pain and names Allah's mercy. The next verse says his prayer was answered.

Dhu'n-Nun, "the man of the fish", is the Prophet Yunus (Jonah), who left his people in anger and was swallowed by a great fish. His prayer from the darkness, la ilaha illa anta subhanaka inni kuntu minaz-zalimin, is widely recited by Muslims in times of distress. The next verse says Allah saved him.

After its long roll call of prophets, Al-Anbiya describes the mission of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ as mercy, rahma. The phrase rahmatan lil-alamin is one of the best-known descriptions of him. "The peoples" renders al-alamin, often understood as all the worlds, the whole of creation.

posts.display_original: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ ٱتَّقُوا۟ رَبَّكُمْ إِنَّ زَلْزَلَةَ ٱلسَّاعَةِ شَىْءٌ عَظِيمٌ
posts.caption: Al-Hajj, "The Pilgrimage", is named for its verses on the pilgrimage to Mecca. It has 78 verses and is usually classed as Medinan, though many scholars see in it a mix of Meccan and Medinan passages. It opens by addressing all humanity; "fear" renders ittaqu, from taqwa, mindful awe of Allah.

The verse asks why people pass the ruins of earlier nations without taking a lesson. Its answer is one of the Quran's best-known lines: real blindness is not of the eyes but of the heart. In Quranic language the heart (qalb) is the seat of understanding, not only of feeling.

Rain falls and by morning the dry ground is green. The Quran often points to this as a sign of Allah's care and of how life returns. "Subtile" renders al-Latif, a name of Allah meaning the Subtle and Gentle, and "Aware" is al-Khabir, the All-Aware.

Near its end, Al-Hajj speaks directly to believers. Its call to bow and prostrate names two movements of the Muslim prayer, ruku' and sujud. Many printed copies of the Quran mark a prostration of recitation at this verse, though the schools of law differ on it.

posts.display: Successful indeed are the believers Who are humble in their prayers, And who shun vain conversation.
posts.display_original: قَدْ أَفْلَحَ ٱلْمُؤْمِنُونَ ٱلَّذِينَ هُمْ فِى صَلَاتِهِمْ خَٰشِعُونَ وَٱلَّذِينَ هُمْ عَنِ ٱللَّغْوِ مُعْرِضُونَ
posts.caption: Al-Mu'minun, "The Believers", is a Meccan surah of 118 verses. It opens with a portrait of the believers, beginning with khushu', humble and focused presence in prayer. The portrait runs on for several more verses and ends with the promise that such people will inherit Paradise.

The Prophet Nuh (Noah) is taught what to pray once he and the believers are aboard the ark: to be brought down at a blessed landing-place. Some Muslims also recite this short prayer, rabbi anzilni munzalan mubarakan, when arriving somewhere new or moving into a new home.

The first sentence is only seven words in Pickthall's English, yet it holds a whole way of answering harm. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, facing mockery and hostility in Mecca, is told to meet bad treatment with something better. The same teaching appears at more length in surah Fussilat (41:34).

Near the end of Al-Mu'minun, those who denied the resurrection are asked a pointed question. The Quran repeatedly insists that creation has a purpose and that every person returns to their Lord. "Deemed ye" means "did you think", and "for naught" means "for nothing" or "in vain".

Al-Mu'minun ends with this short prayer for forgiveness and mercy, which the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is told to say. It echoes the prayer of the believers a few verses earlier, whom the arrogant had mocked. Many Muslims recite it as a simple everyday prayer.

posts.display: Let them forgive and show indulgence. Yearn ye not that Allah may forgive you? Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
posts.display_original: وَلْيَعْفُوا۟ وَلْيَصْفَحُوٓا۟ أَلَا تُحِبُّونَ أَن يَغْفِرَ ٱللَّهُ لَكُمْ وَٱللَّهُ غَفُورٌ رَّحِيمٌ
posts.caption: An-Nur, "The Light", is a Medinan surah of 64 verses. According to classical commentators, this verse came after a believer vowed to stop supporting a poor relative who had joined in spreading a slander, and on hearing it he resumed his help. The verse ties the two together: those who hope to be forgiven are asked to forgive.

posts.display: Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The similitude of His light is as a niche wherein is a lamp. The lamp is in a glass. The glass is as it were a shining star.
posts.display_original: ٱللَّهُ نُورُ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ مَثَلُ نُورِهِۦ كَمِشْكَوٰةٍ فِيهَا مِصْبَاحٌ ٱلْمِصْبَاحُ فِى زُجَاجَةٍ ٱلزُّجَاجَةُ كَأَنَّهَا كَوْكَبٌ دُرِّىٌّ
posts.caption: The opening of the Light Verse (Ayat an-Nur), which gives An-Nur its name. It goes on to describe a lamp lit from a blessed olive tree whose oil almost glows by itself, "light upon light". Scholars and poets have written at length on this one verse; al-Ghazali devoted a book, The Niche of Lights, to it.

posts.display: Men whom neither merchandise nor sale beguileth from remembrance of Allah and constancy in prayer and paying to the poor their due; who fear a day when hearts and eyeballs will be overturned.
posts.caption: The verse before speaks of houses of worship where Allah's name is remembered morning and evening. These are the people found there: trade and business never distract them from remembering Allah, from prayer, or from giving zakat, the obligatory alms that Pickthall renders "paying to the poor their due".

The verse pictures all of creation, down to birds with their wings outspread, offering its own kind of worship and praise. "In their flight" renders the Arabic saffat, with wings spread wide. It is one of several verses describing the whole universe as glorifying Allah.

posts.display: But when ye enter houses, salute one another with a greeting from Allah, blessed and sweet.
posts.display_original: فَإِذَا دَخَلْتُم بُيُوتًا فَسَلِّمُوا۟ عَلَىٰٓ أَنفُسِكُمْ تَحِيَّةً مِّنْ عِندِ ٱللَّهِ مُبَٰرَكَةً طَيِّبَةً
posts.caption: This line comes near the end of a verse about sharing meals in the homes of relatives and friends. Muslims understand the greeting from Allah as the salam: as-salamu alaykum, "peace be upon you". The Arabic literally says "greet yourselves", which commentators explain as greeting one another.

posts.display_original: تَبَارَكَ ٱلَّذِى نَزَّلَ ٱلْفُرْقَانَ عَلَىٰ عَبْدِهِۦ لِيَكُونَ لِلْعَٰلَمِينَ نَذِيرًا
posts.caption: Al-Furqan, a Meccan surah of 77 verses, takes its name from this verse. Al-Furqan, "the Criterion", is a name for the Quran: the standard that separates truth from falsehood. "His slave" means His servant, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, sent as a warner to all peoples.

posts.display: The (faithful) slaves of the Beneficent are they who walk upon the earth modestly, and when the foolish ones address them answer: Peace.
posts.caption: The closing passage of Al-Furqan describes Ibad ar-Rahman, "the servants of the Most Merciful". It begins with how they walk, humbly, and how they answer people who speak to them rudely or ignorantly: with words of peace. Pickthall's "slaves" renders ibad, servants or worshippers.

After naming grave sins, the passage makes an exception for anyone who repents, believes and does good. Many Muslims count this among the most hopeful lines in the Quran: for those who turn back, Allah changes their bad deeds into good ones.

The servants of the Most Merciful pray that their families will be a comfort to them, literally a "coolness of the eyes" (qurrat a'yun), an Arabic image of deep contentment. Many Muslims recite it as a prayer for their homes. That closes this journey from Maryam to Al-Furqan; thank you for reading along.
